rationale: A wins because it gives the founder sharper strategic material and polices its own weak spots instead of laundering them into headlines. A's "A 22% drop in no-shows is the number the fitness industry has been guessing at for years" correctly makes the data the story and demands the methodology before pitching. B has usable bones, but "Mindbody owns both the studio's booking system and ClassPass — now its AI sits on top of both" overstates the supplied facts; the update does not say the assistant touches ClassPass at all.
gaps_in_A: "studios get it whether or not they asked for it" stretches "pricing is bundled into existing software tiers" into implied automatic rollout or adoption.
"The company that owns ClassPass now decides which classes fill first" is punchy but too declarative; the facts say texting waitlisted members and suggesting class times, not demand prioritization.
"Take-private, then automate: what Mindbody is building away from public disclosure" is interesting but thin; the PE value-creation frame needs outside proof the update does not supply.
gaps_in_B: "cut studio no-show rates 22% by texting the waitlist" turns a company-claimed pilot result into causation; the facts do not prove texting caused the drop.
"using aggregated booking data across the network" invents aggregation and network-wide data use; the update only says booking data.
"now its AI sits on top of both" is an overclaim unless the assistant interacts with ClassPass inventory, which B itself admits is unknown.
The next step, "journalist-fit-check," is premature. Pilot methodology and a named studio are the gate before list-building, not an errand after it.
